Module This chapter is part of the DP Module ("Dénombrement et Probabilités", that is, "Counting, Enumerating and Probabilities"). The prerequisites are: the LE Module ("Logic and Sets", seen during the seminar). Motivation « Counting » is a frequent activity for a computer scientist: counting the number of bits required to stock an integer number in a computer, counting the number of elementary operations required when executing an algorithm, counting the number of words of a given length that can be obtained from a finite alphabet, counting the number of connected or biconnected components in a graph, etc. This work is often related to the notion of « estimating » a number: indeed, it is sometimes difficult to get the exact number of realizations of the studied phenomenon, so we just try to find an upper or a lower bound, depending on our reason for counting. This estimation consists in getting the number of realizations in the best or worst case 1 . For example, when executing a brute force implementation to compute the Fibonacci sequence, it is difficult to predict the exact number of recursive calls. It is easier to get a lower and an upper bound for this number, both of them depending on the rank of the Fibonacci term we're computing. In the same way, when determining the GCD of two numbers, it is easier to get an upper bound for the number of Euclidean divisions that will be required, rather than getting this exact number. The latter is indeed very difficult to determine. Our purpose in the following is to bring you to a practical experience of counting . From a mathematical point of view, this work consists in enumerating ; the latter point refers to the lecture. It is a transversal activity. Answering the exercises will require you to employ many skills that you have developed in your past and new skills that we will develop now. These skills will be a great help for further activities, such as determining the complexity of algorithms or studying finite probability distributions. Learning outcomes As a general rule, we expect you to enumerate and count finite sets which can be handled by combinations, arrangements and permutations. The detailed learning outcomes are: • count the number of ways of picking elements from a finite set, with or without replacement, with or without repetitions; • count the number of mappings from a finite set to another; • adapt the typical methods to real life situations; • expand a binomial expression to a power n \in \mathbb{N} ; • prove the Pascal's formula, using either a counting or a computational method; • prove the binomial formula, using either a counting or a computational method; • imagine simple situations associated to a given way of counting. Some of these skills are transversal. Our main objective is that you engage in thinking and searching : considering hypotheses, testing them, finding counter examples. 1 It is hence different from a statistical estimation.

section: 1 Cardinal number of a finite set
content: 1 Cardinal number of a finite set 1.1 Summary Solving a counting problem consists in determining the number of elements in a given set. The first two sections rely on this point. The first section focuses on the behavior of the cardinal numbers 2 of sets when combined with the usual operations, while the second section deals with the modeling/formalization process: we will try to extract the main abstract ideas that may lead to the solution. This section is also the opportunity to apply some of the results about sets that we have seen before. Here, these concepts should be more tangible; it should be easier for you to try to feel your way toward the solution, using counter examples and building your own representations of sets and functions. You will note that, for some of the exercises, there are several ways to solve them. Typically, a direct method and a recursive method. It is important to understand the advantages and draw-backs of both ways of thinking 3 . On the one hand, the direct methods lead to explicit formulas, which directly provide all the information we're looking for (order of magnitude, comparisons). Yet they require a global understanding of the problem we are trying to solve. These methods are, hence, difficult to implement, but their results are easy to use. On the other hand, recursive methods provide the evolution of the result with the size of the problem, rather than the explicit result. If you really need the latter, you still have extra work to do in order to get an explicit formula. But implementing these methods requires only a local understanding of the problem, the underlying reasoning is more natural. Recursive methods are, hence, easier to implement, but their results are more difficult to use. In mathematics, we usually prefer an explicit formula which directly provides a numerical answer to a problem. It is not always true, however, when programming: a recursive formula can easily lead to a numerical answer, after entering into a loop which will quickly compute the successive intermediate values until the final one 4 . Many algorithmic tools (dynamic programming, memoization, etc.) enable this way of computing the final result. 1.2 Exercises Exercise 1.1 Let A (and B ) be the set of natural numbers which are multiples of 2 (and 3), smaller than or equal to 60. • What are the cardinal numbers of A and B ? • What can you say about the cardinal number of A \cap B ? • What is the cardinal number of A \times B ? The cardinal number of A \cup B ? Exercise 1.2 Let M and A denote the final grades in math and in algorithmics in S1 of EPITA. Both grades are between 0 and 20 and we suppose that they have integer values. Assuming that both modules have the same coefficient, a student tries to determine the number of combinations of A and M which may result in a global average equal to k \in \{1, \dots, 20\} . How can you help this student? You may, for example, represent the situation with a 2-entries table. Exercise 1.3 We focus on the cardinal number of the union of two sets A and B , whose intersection may be non-empty. 2 The most common ways to denote the cardinal number of a set A are: \text{Card}(A) , |A| , \#(A) etc. 3 The chapter about numerical sequences will raise this question again. 4 Paradoxically, you will see mathematical situations, such as the computation of a matrix determinant, where a recursive formula is more convenient than the explicit formula. Sometimes, the recursive method consists in a succession of easy to understand calculations, while the explicit formula is not tractable.

again one of the few basic questions. The difficult point is to make the connection between the real-life situation and the right basic question. In computer science, it is frequent to think in terms of «class of problems»: if a problem can be reduced, that is, if it can be formulated as another well-known problem, then we say that both problems are equivalent and have the same underlying solution. That's why during class, we will work with abstract descriptions of the exercises: how do we connect the exercise to one of the reference problems? And how do we solve this reference problem? We will hence focus on the relation between the intuitive and the formal representations of different problems. 2.2 Exercises Exercise 2.7 1. A bag contains n balls, numbered from 1 to n . • We successively pick k balls from the bag, with replacement. How many possible ways of picking the balls? • We successively pick n balls from the bag, without replacement. How many possible ways of picking the balls? • We successively pick k balls from the bag, without replacement ( k \leq n ). How many possible ways of picking the balls? • We simultaneously pick k balls from the bag ( k \leq n ) and put them in another bag. How many possible results? 2. Let E be a n -element set and k \leq n . What is a k -element arrangement of E ? A permutation of E ? A k -element combination of E ? How many are there? Exercise 2.8 Find the numbers of • anagrams with the word computer • anagrams with the word mathematician • ways of calling 5 students from this class one by one to the blackboard. That is, the number of ways of choosing the 5 students and their order of call. • ways of calling all the students from this class one by one to the blackboard. • ways of calling all the students from this class one by one to the blackboard, given that the two students who came late this morning will be called twice. Exercise 2.9 A football club has a 24-player squad and the coach has to select the 11 players who will start the next match. Find the number of possible choices for the coach in the following situations: 1. Everyone in the squad can play at any position (goalkeeper, defender, midfielder, etc.). The coach just decides who plays, disregarding the positions of the players. 2. Everyone in the squad can play at any position. But the coach decides who plays and at which position. 3. Answer the previous questions if, from the squad, 3 players can only be goalkeepers while the 21 others can be at any position except goalkeeper.

Exercise 2.10 An association has 100 members. They have to select a 10-councilor board. Each councilor must be a member and the board will have: • A president • A treasurer • 8 other councilors No councilor can be at two positions simultaneously in the board. 1. How many possible boards are possible? 2. Answer the same question if, furthermore, the gender-parity is required. Assume the the members are 50 women, 50 men. If the president is a women, the treasurer must be a man and reversely. The other councilors must be 4 women, 4 men. Exercise 2.11 Let k and n be two non-zero natural numbers. For each of the following formulas, suggest a counting problem whose solution is the given formula 6 : • 2^n • \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} • k \cdot (n!) 3 Combinatorics 3.1 Summary Combinatorics deals with the different ways to rank finite sets or subsets: permutations, arrangements and combinations. These are often used as modeling processes for random experiments: picking cards, betting on the horses before a race and so on. It is natural then to apply these methods to finite probabilities: under the assumption of equiprobability of each possible result 7 , a finite probability question can be seen as a problem of getting the numbers of positive and possible results, the final probability being the ratio of these two numbers. These methods may also be applied to get an exhaustive enumeration of some sets: how many binary trees will fulfill a given property, or how many paths exist in a graph. Such enumerations can lead to an estimation of the complexity of some brute force algorithms (such as backtracking algorithms). 6 \binom{n}{k} can also be denoted by C_n^k (and not C_k^n ). You're expected to know both notations; they can be used in future works, MCQ, exams and so on. 7 When the results are not equiprobable, their enumeration and their relative frequencies enable the same reasoning.

3.2 Exercises ★ Exercise 3.12 This exercise is about the «permutations» of the set \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket , that is to say the bijections from this set into itself. 1. What is the total number of permutations of \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket ? 2. Show that the composition of two permutations of \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket is a permutation of \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket . 3. Let f be a permutation of \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket . Show that there exist two distinct natural numbers p and q such that f^p = f^q . 4. Deduce that there exists a natural number r > 0 such that f^r = id_{\llbracket 1, n \rrbracket} . Exercise 3.13 The bookshelf of an EPITA student, reserved for «cramming» for the next exam, contains 4 algo books, 6 math books and 3 physics books. Determine the number of ways to rank them on the shelf, given that they must be classified according to the subject they refer to. Exercise 3.14 Let n \in \mathbb{N}^* and k \in \llbracket 0, n \rrbracket . 1. Compare the number of ways of choosing a subset of k elements from a set of n , with the number of ways of choosing a subset of n - k elements. Can you explain the resulting property? 2. In a box, there are n balls numbered 1 to n . We simultaneously pick k balls ( k \geq 1 ). (a) How many possible results are possible? (b) From these results, how many contain the 1-ball? (c) How many results don't have the 1-ball? (d) Deduce a relation between \binom{n}{k} , \binom{n-1}{k} and \binom{n-1}{k-1} . (e) Prove this relation with a computation. Exercise 3.16 Consider the following sum: \sum_{k=0}^n 2^k \binom{n}{k} . • Compute its value. • Find a problem whose answer is equal to this sum. Exercise 3.17 A candidate came to the Advance exam by bicycle. He locked his bike at the gate of the school, using a padlock with 4 digits (from 0 to 9). Then the math teacher asked him: 1. a. What is the number of possibilities for the padlock's code? b. What is the number of possibilities whose last digit is even? c. What is the number of possibilities which contain at least once the digit 2? 2. Suppose now that the code is made of 4 mutually distinct digits. a. What is the number of possibilities for the padlock's code? b. What is the number of possibilities whose last digit is even? c. What is the number of possibilities which contain at least once the digit 2? 4 In your programming activity 4.1 Summary Algorithmics and programming raise numerous counting problems. Here are some typical examples: • estimation of the number of iterations in a loop, or of how many times the loop will enter into a specified conditional instruction • estimation of the number of bits required to stock a natural number in memory • for a sorting algorithm, estimation of the input size, of the number of possible outputs, of the proportion of operations involving some specified sub-lists • words manipulation in language theory • estimation of the number of paths between two points in a graph. We suggest that you ask your algorithmics and programming teachers how these questions arise in their practical work. You may have been faced with some of them before; you will certainly be in the future. 4.2 Exercises Exercise 4.18 Let a and b be two natural numbers. 1. How many elements are there in \llbracket a, b \rrbracket ? 2. How many even elements in \llbracket 2, 10 \rrbracket and in \llbracket 2, 13 \rrbracket ? 1. a. What is the number of possibilities for the padlock's code? b. What is the number of possibilities whose last digit is even? c. What is the number of possibilities which contain at least once the digit 2? 2. Suppose now that the code is made of 4 mutually distinct digits. a.
